newsitem.title: USA: Intel reports second quarter profit.
newsitem.headline: Intel reports second quarter profit.

text.p: Semiconductor maker Intel Corp. reported sharply higher second-quarter profits on Tuesday despite a drop in demand for some of the company's older-generation products.

In a statement issued after markets closed, the Santa Clara, Calif.-based maker of microprocessors and other computer products reported net income of $1.6 billion, or 92 cents a share, compared with $1.0 billion, or 59 cents a share, a year ago. The per share figures for both periods reflect a 2-for-1 stock split that took effect earlier this week. Revenues rose to $6.0 billion from $4.6 billion.

The earnings figure topped analyst's consensus estimate of 90 cents per share and was well above Wall Street's recent "whisper number" circulating around trading rooms that the result could be a few pennies a share weaker than that.

As the company had warned on May 30, revenues and earnings during the seasonally slower second quarter were down from the first quarter due to a combination of weakness in Europe and the introduction of new microprocessors.

"Strong microprocessor shipments in the first quarter led to some inventory correction in the second quarter as the industry prepared for a rapid transition to (Pentium) processors with MMX (multimedia) technology," Intel Chairman Andrew Grove said.
Shares of Intel rose to $81.50 in after-hours trading. The stock closed up $2.15625 at $80.90625.

Intel said it expects third-quarter revenues to be flat to slightly higher than the $6.0 billion of revenues it posted in the second quarter. Gross margins would be flat to slightly lower than the second quarter's 61 percent.
Intel's 1997 capital spending estimate remained at $4.5 billion, and the company still expects gross margins for the full year to be at 60 percent, plus or minus a few points.

The outlook was toward the positive side of what analysts had been expecting, with some concerned the company could warn of a deeper expected decline in gross margins in the September quarter, or that revenues might not pick up sequentially.
"It doesn't look bad," said C.B. Lee, an analyst at Sutro & Co., noting some analysts had warned Intel's second-quarter results could miss the Wall Street consensus figure.
But Lee also said Intel's earnings per share estimates for the September quarter will likely be reduced, as several analysts have been predicting.
Lee noted the company expects interest and other income for the third quarter will be around $140 million, down from $212 million in the second quarter, for example.
The company said it bought back a total of 13.0 million of its common shares at a cost of $945 million.
Intel Chief Financial Officer Andy Bryant told Reuters the company has continued to buy back shares as part of an ongoing program.
"We believe a good use of the cash is to buy back our own stock. We think it's a pretty good investment," he said.
Intel had warned investors on May 30 that it expected results in the second quarter to fall short of its previous expectations.

Intel's results follow statements of weaker-than-expected results from chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Cyrix Corp., which are beginning to give the company competition for the first time in years.
Like Intel, those chipmakers are also dealing with a rapid shift to newer generation microprocessors and feeling pricing pressures on their older computer chips, which are being phased out.

Intel chief Andrew Grove has described the product transition as "monumental" and recently estimated that by the fourth quarter, about 90 percent of Intel's microprocessor revenues will come from its Pentium with MMX technology and new Pentium II processors.
"Demand for the Pentium processor with MMX technology and the Pentium II processor is strong, and we are ramping production at a record rate," he said Tuesday.
(sam.perry@reuters.com, in Palo Alto, +1 415-845 5400)
